Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Kwame is a 37-year-old African American psychologist who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to manage on his own. He works in an outpatient mental health clinic, where he is used to listening carefully to other people's suffering and helping them make sense of overwhelming experiences. Since the assault, that professional role has become harder to inhabit. What happened to him occurred when he was alone with another man in a locked room, and the details that remain most alive for him are not broad impressions but specific conditions: the click of the lock, the sense of the walls closing in, the unmistakable fact of being trapped with a male body between him and the door. In recounting it, he does not embellish. He says he knew, in those moments, that he could not get out, and what stays with him now is the certainty he felt then that he was completely at another person's mercy.

In the weeks afterward, he returned to work and tried to move through his days as if discipline and routine might contain what had happened. Instead, parts of ordinary life began to feel charged in ways he could not ignore. If a door shut behind him in an office or consultation room, even briefly, his body reacted before he had time to think. He became acutely aware of whether he could leave, whether the handle worked, whether someone else was between him and the exit. If he found himself alone with a male colleague in a small room, he felt the familiar surge of alarm and the immediate need to reposition himself. He began choosing chairs with his back against the wall, arranging himself so he could see the whole room and the door at once. In team meetings he would arrive early for the seat he considered safest, and if it was taken he struggled to follow the discussion, scanning instead who was behind him, who was near the door, how quickly he could stand up if he needed to.

His work exposes him to conversations that now land with particular force. A passing comment about sexual violence in case conference, a patient's disclosure, even hearing male staff discuss such topics in a detached professional tone can suddenly pull him into the felt reality of the assault. He has not described elaborate flashbacks; rather, there is an abrupt shift in him, as if the room becomes less solidly present and his body remembers confinement and danger. He goes quiet, keeps his face composed, and waits for the moment to pass. Over time he has started avoiding situations he believes might corner him into these reactions. He leaves some discussions early, declines opportunities that would place him alone with male coworkers, and prefers doors left cracked open whenever possible. These habits have narrowed his day. Colleagues have noticed him as more distant and rigid, though they do not know why.

At home, the same watchfulness continues. He has difficulty falling asleep because lying down feels too much like surrendering awareness. He stays alert into the night, listening for sounds, reluctant to let himself drift off. Even when he tells himself he is in his own apartment and there is no immediate threat, he cannot fully relax. He checks where exits are, notices how enclosed a space feels, and settles only in positions where he can monitor the room. He is single, and the isolation of going home alone has sharpened his sense that there is no one who can reliably protect him. He has come to believe, with a bleak certainty, that he cannot stop bad things from happening to him. Alongside that is another conviction he finds humiliating and hard to dismiss: that what happened is somehow visible, that other people can look at him and know. In the clinic hallway, in the elevator, in the grocery store, he catches himself wondering whether he appears marked or exposed.

Over the months this has hardened into a feeling of hopelessness he struggles to name aloud. He has begun to think of the future in shortened terms, not with plans but with endurance. For someone whose work depends on presence, steadiness, and trust, the contrast with his inner life has become unbearable. What finally brought him to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of small moments he could no longer explain away: changing seats yet again in a meeting so his back was protected, losing sleep night after night, feeling his body tense when a male colleague closed the office door, and then hearing a discussion of sexual assault at work and realizing he could barely remain in the room. He came in ashamed of needing treatment as a psychologist, but more frightened of what would happen if he continued living as though every closed room and every solitary moment with a man might become dangerous. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened, but to stop feeling as if he is still trapped inside it and to believe, even a little, that his life is not already over.
